patch.value: A defect the tracker considers closed keeps blocking releases: nothing joins a closed item to the observability issue whose rolling window gates the cut

The release gate reads a rolling 14-day activity window over unresolved observability issues, so an error stops blocking a cut only when someone dispositions it in the external system. Nothing joins the two records. Closing the pm item that owns a defect has no effect on the issue that gates the release, and resolving the issue leaves no trace in the immutable record, so the tracker can report a defect fixed while the release stays red for that same defect, and it can report a defect open while the release is green because the window rolled past it. Measured 2026-08-07: the scheduled cut failed on exactly one blocking issue whose product behaviour was correct, and after the product fix landed the cut still required a manual disposition in a system this repository never writes to. The pieces to close the loop already exist and are unused. The release workflow creates a release object and associates commits with it, so resolve-in-next-release is semantically available; the handled-error channel already tags every event with the error code; and items already carry the observability short identifier in their titles. What is missing is the relation and the automation over it: no dependency kind, no field, and no gate connects a tracked defect to the observability record whose lifetime gates the release. This is a broken turn of the self-improvement loop, because the loop cannot re-measure an improvement whose gate lives outside the record.

A tracked defect and the observability issue that gates the release are joined by a recorded relation, so the join is readable from the immutable record rather than from a title substring; Closing the owning item dispositions the joined observability issue, and the disposition is recorded as a mutation rather than performed silently out of band; The release gate reports, for every blocking issue, whether a tracked item claims to have fixed it, so a red cut names the item that disagrees with it; A negative control proves an unjoined blocking issue still fails the gate, so the join can never be used to waive an untracked error

value.text:
Reference instance recorded 2026-08-10, and it is the cleanest reproduction of this item so far because the fix and the block happened on the same day.

The observability issue PM-CLI-2X, titled as an ENOTDIR fault opening a path, was the root cause fixed by the tracker-root guard reachability work earlier that day: an optional read of the context intents file tolerated only ENOENT and threw a raw ENOTDIR before the typed guard could classify it. The product fix shipped. The Sentry issue was left unresolved, because nothing connects the two.

The scheduled cut at 04:15Z then failed. The reliability gate reported one high-severity issue inside its fourteen-day window, blocking short id PM-CLI-2X, reason unexpected_fault, threshold_ok false. So the daily release was blocked by a fault that no longer existed in the code being released, and the gate was correct on its own terms every step of the way: the issue was genuinely unresolved, genuinely inside the window, and genuinely classified as an unexpected fault, because the event that carried that classification was recorded before the fix and is immutable.

Three facts about the recovery are worth keeping. The block cleared only when the Sentry issue was resolved by hand, not when the fix landed. The workflow already creates a Sentry release object during the release job, so resolve-in-next-release is available in the same pipeline that blocked, which is the mechanism this item proposes and it remains unused. And the window is what converts a one-off into a recurrence: an unresolved issue keeps blocking for fourteen days regardless of how long ago the code was repaired, so a single missed resolution can block up to fourteen consecutive daily cuts.

That last property explains the shape of the failure clustering measured on pm-e70zh5 the same day. Eleven of the forty most recent scheduled runs failed, and the failures arrive in clusters rather than uniformly, with four failures in the six days ending 08-10. A per-occurrence view reads each of those as an independent incident to be repaired; a windowed gate over unresolved issues predicts precisely that clustering, because one unresolved record blocks repeatedly until someone notices it is stale.

The join this item asks for is therefore not only a convenience. It is what makes the release gate's window measure current reliability rather than the age of an unclosed record.

value.text: New reference instance 2026-08-20: Sentry PM-CLI-37 captured one handled dependency-kind-blocks-not-found error while pm-c90tfh was actively introducing that tracker assertion. PR #1069 fixed the source and merged as c839c4df3; Sentry was then resolved against that exact commit. The join was again reconstructed manually from event time, assertion name, PM history, PR, and commit because no typed PM-to-observability relation or automatic closeout exists, directly confirming this open item without creating a duplicate.
